issue.title: turbo-persistence: cover block lengths in CRCs
issue.body:
## Summary

Stacked on #100313.

The 8-byte headers of SST blocks and blob files store `[uncompressed_length][crc32]`, but the CRC only covered the payload. A corrupted length therefore passed the checksum check and could:

- make a reader allocate a decompression buffer of up to 4 GB;
- flip whether a block is treated as compressed (`0` means uncompressed).

The CRC now covers the four big-endian length bytes followed by the on-disk payload. `checksum_block(uncompressed_length, data)` hashes both incrementally with `crc32fast::Hasher`, so no extra copy is made.

Readers verify this checksum before using the length to allocate decompression output or to choose the decompression path. That covers:

- SST lookups in mmap and file mode, plus file-backed decoded iteration and the index block read with `pread`;
- blob reads;
- `sst_inspect`.

The index block's checksum is now verified before its sentinel check, so a corrupted index length is reported as a checksum error.

The on-disk layout is unchanged, but the meaning of the checksum changes. Caches written by older builds fail validation and are treated as cache corruption.

Iteration still passes medium value blocks to compaction as raw bytes without decompressing them. Their original length and CRC are preserved through the copy, so a corrupted block is detected when the copied value is read. The README documents the new checksum coverage for SST blocks and blob files.

Not covered: a CRC detects accidental corruption, not tampering. There is no cap on the output size, and no compatibility reader for old caches.

## Verification

Tests that corrupt only the length header, with offsets left valid:

- SST blocks: lookups in mmap and file mode and decoded iteration with `pread`, including compressed-to-uncompressed and uncompressed-to-compressed sentinel corruption.
- The compaction raw-copy path.
- Blob reads in mmap and file mode.
- `sst_inspect`.

Commands run:

- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence --all-targets`
- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence --features strict_checks`
- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence --no-default-features`
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-persistence --all-targets`, with the default features, with `--no-default-features` and with `--features strict_checks`
- `cargo check -p turbo-tasks-backend`
- Miri with the CI flags, on the new length, raw-copy and checksum tests and the offset-corruption test.

Before this change, small length corruptions in blob files were caught only by the decompressor, not by the checksum check.

issue.title: turbo-tasks-backend: merge aggregated data updates for new followers
issue.body:
### What?

Resolves the `TODO merge AggregatedDataUpdate` in `inner_of_upper_has_new_followers` (turbo-tasks-backend aggregation update queue). The diffs produced while connecting several new followers to an upper are now merged into a single `AggregatedDataUpdate`, and at most one `AggregatedDataUpdateJob` is enqueued for the upper's uppers.

### Why?

When an upper gains N new inner followers, applying their data produced up to N diffs, and each one was enqueued as its own job with a clone of the same `upper_ids`. Every one of those jobs then locks and updates each grand-upper separately, even though a single combined update has the same net effect.

### How?

- New `AggregatedDataUpdate::merge`:
  - Dirty container updates are summed per field. All diffs returned by `apply` on the same task carry that task's id, which is a documented precondition and checked with a debug assertion. If the sums cancel to zero, the dirty container update is dropped.
  - Collectible entries are concatenated. The existing `optimize` then sums them per collectible and drops zero entries, so `+1`/`-1` pairs from successive diffs cancel.
- At the call site, the diffs are merged and optimized after the upper's lock is released. The optimize pass is skipped when there is only a single diff. Nothing is enqueued if the merged update is empty or the upper has no uppers.
- Applying the merged update gives the same final counts and the same net presence changes as applying the diffs one after another. Only intermediate flips that cancel out are skipped, the same guarantee `optimize` already relies on. How incoming updates are applied to the upper itself, including dirty scheduling and collectible invalidation, is unchanged.

### Verification

- New unit tests cover summed dirty counts, cancellation, collectible summing/cancellation, and merging with empty updates.
- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend`, `cargo clippy -p turbo-tasks-backend --all-targets`, and `cargo fmt --check` pass.

issue.title: turbo-persistence: validate sst_inspect block reads with BlockOffsets
issue.body:
## Summary

#100288 moved SST block-directory validation into `BlockOffsets`: the whole directory is read with `pread` and validated once when a file is opened, and every block read goes through `BlockOffsets::block_range`. That covers the runtime readers this PR originally hardened. What's left here is the `sst_inspect` tool, which still read SST files with unchecked arithmetic, plus end-to-end tests.

- **`sst_inspect` reuses the runtime validation.** `BlockOffsets` is now public, with `read` and `block_range` (both documented). `sst_inspect` builds its block directory with `BlockOffsets::read` and locates every block through `block_range`. Before this change it panicked on several kinds of corrupt file:

  | Corrupt file | Before |
  | --- | --- |
  | File shorter than its block directory | subtract with overflow |
  | Zero blocks | `block_count - 1` overflow |
  | Out-of-range block offset | slice panic |
  | Out-of-range block index | slice panic |
  | Index block ending inside the directory | reported as a checksum mismatch |

  All of these now return a descriptive error.
- **Zero-block files.** `BlockOffsets::read` accepts an empty directory, and the runtime rejects it separately when reading the index block. `sst_inspect` now rejects zero blocks explicitly before it looks for the index block.
- **Decompressed-length mismatch.** In `sst_inspect` this returns an error instead of failing an `assert_eq!`.
- **End-to-end open tests (coverage only).** These open corrupt files through `StaticSortedFile::open` in every lookup access mode and through the file-backed `StaticSortedFileIter::open` (iteration uses `pread` since #100336):
  - empty and truncated files;
  - zero blocks;
  - an index block that is past the end, overlaps the directory, is too short, ends before it starts, or is header-only;
  - a real SST with each non-index directory entry corrupted.

  Current canary already rejects all of these, so they only guard against regressions.

Runtime reader behavior is unchanged.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence --all-targets`, plus runs with `--features strict_checks` and with `--no-default-features`.
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-persistence --all-targets` in all three configurations, and `cargo doc` with `-D warnings`.
- On canary without this change:
  - the new `sst_inspect` tests fail as listed above;
  - the runtime open tests pass when only the test code is applied.

issue.title: Turbopack: add build cache portability e2e test and fix location-dependent tasks
issue.body:
### What?

Adds an e2e test that checks whether the Turbopack filesystem build cache survives moving the project to another directory. It also fixes the first portability problems the test found.

Stacked on #101025, which adds the `executions` counter to turbo-tasks task statistics that this test relies on.

### Why?

A restored build cache should still be valid when the project sits at a different absolute path. That happens with CI checkouts, Docker build contexts, and caches restored into another workspace. Today, moving a project makes many tasks re-execute even though nothing changed. This PR adds a way to measure that and removes some of the causes.

### How?

**Test** (`test/e2e/app-dir/turbopack-portable-build-cache`, Turbopack production builds only, not deploy):

- Each case runs a cold `next build`, a warm build in the same directory, then moves the whole project root (including `.next`) and runs another warm build.
- Every build writes turbo-tasks task statistics (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TASK_STATISTICS`) to a temporary file outside the project. The test collects the functions with `executions > 0`.
  - `cache_miss` isn't enough: it only counts newly created tasks, while a restored task that re-executes after an invalidation counts as a cache hit. #101025 adds the `executions` counter.
- Inline snapshots record the sorted executed function names for the same-dir and moved builds. All `NextConfig` methods are collapsed into a single `NextConfig::*` entry: they depend on the same config cell, and which ones are called depends on the build mode. The snapshots document the current state, and the moved diff should shrink as portability improves. A cold-build execution count check makes sure an empty snapshot means "cached", not "nothing counted".
- Two fixtures:
  - a minimal app;
  - a monorepo whose workspace root is the project root. It covers app and pages routes, a route handler, SSG, a server action, client components from a workspace package, proxy, a `turbopack.rules` loader, `resolveAlias`, jsconfig `paths` outside the app, and relative symlinks.

  The test asserts the route table, the server-actions manifest, and rendered markers on both builds, so a silently dropped feature can't make a snapshot look clean.
- The build env pins `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Inside Docker, `getStorageDirectory()` doesn't persist the generated key in `.next/cache`, so each build would produce a new one. The key is a Turbopack project input, so this would invalidate server-action-dependent work and make snapshots environment-dependent and nondeterministic.
- To keep the snapshots environment-independent, the test also:
  - always installs with pnpm's hoisted linker. The default layout depends on the Node.js version (realpath workaround), which changes which symlinks are resolved;
  - disables telemetry, which reads extra config values.

**Turbopack fixes**, so tasks don't depend on the absolute project location:

- **Source map rewriting** (`turbopack-core` `source_map/utils.rs`):
  - It used to await the entire `DiskFileSystem`, whose cell includes the absolute root, just to build the `turbopack:///[name]/` prefix.
  - It now reads only the filesystem name, through its own task. It reads it only when a source actually uses that prefix, and needs the root only for absolute-path conversion.
  - This removed all relocation-only codegen re-execution (`module_factory_with_code_generation_issue` / `EcmascriptChunkItemContent::new`) in the minimal app.
- **`WriteLinkContent::hash`** reads only the filesystem name instead of the whole filesystem, and no longer requires a `DiskFileSystem`. Hash values are unchanged.
- **`resolve_options`** checks for the configured tsconfig with `get_type()` instead of `metadata()`. A failed `metadata` call's error includes the absolute path, and errors are part of the task output, so the check used to change after a move:
  - files and symlinks count as present;
  - directories, missing entries, and read errors fall back to tsconfig discovery.
- The `trace_task_dirty` feature compiles again (`task_id` was undefined in `make_task_dirty_without_scheduling`).

**Remaining after a move** (visible in the moved snapshots):

- `NextConfig::*` re-runs (`from_string` and its getters), because the serialized config contains absolute paths (`turbopack.root`, `outputFileTracingRoot`, …).
- `DiskFileSystem::new_internal` and writes to the new output location re-run.
- The webpack-loader evaluation pool re-runs; it needs absolute paths to launch Node.js.

### Verification

- Both portability cases pass twice in a row with `CI=1`, and once more with `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS=true`, on top of #101025. The task-statistics snapshots list the same functions as the earlier trace-based ones.
- Existing `server-source-maps`, `tsconfig-path`, `typescript-custom-tsconfig` and `tsconfig-module-preserve` e2e tests pass.
- Rust tests and Turbopack snapshot tests for the touched crates pass.
- Clippy, `pnpm typescript`, prettier and eslint are clean.
- Only measured on Linux x64.

issue.title: turbo-tasks: count task executions in task statistics
issue.body:
### What?

Adds an `executions` counter to turbo-tasks task statistics (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TASK_STATISTICS`). It counts how often a task of each function started executing.

```json
"next_core::next_config::NextConfig::from_string": { "cache_hit": 1, "cache_miss": 0, "executions": 1 }
```

- **What's counted:** `cache_hit` / `cache_miss` count function calls that found or created a task, as before. `executions` counts actual executions, including re-executions of existing tasks after an invalidation.
- **Where:** the counter is recorded in `try_start_task_execution` once a cached task has been taken from `Scheduled` and is about to run. Transient root tasks have no function and aren't counted.
- **Cost:** there's no overhead beyond the existing `Option` check when statistics are disabled.
- **Test:** a new test in `turbo-tasks-backend/tests/task_statistics.rs` covers fresh executions, cache hits without execution, and a re-execution after an invalidation whose lookup still counts as a hit.

### Why?

`cache_miss` only counts a task *type* that isn't in memory or the persistent cache. A restored task that is dirty re-executes, but its callers record a `cache_hit`, so the statistics can't show which work a warm build actually redid.

Example: in #100780, moving a project with its build cache re-runs `NextConfig::from_string` and 13 other functions, yet the statistics report **no** misses. With `executions`, the statistics show exactly the functions that a turbo-tasks trace shows. The portability test can then use the cheap JSON instead of parsing a trace.

## Summary
Fixes an issue where `create-next-app` would omit the available commands and next-steps guidance (`npm run dev`, `npm run build`, `npm start`, `cd <project>`) after scaffolding an app from a template.

## Why
In `packages/create-next-app/create-app.ts`, `hasPackageJson` was initialized to `false` and only updated within the `if (example)` branch. In the `else` branch (templates), `hasPackageJson` was never set to `true`, causing the final `if (hasPackageJson)` check to evaluate to `false` and silently skip printing the command instructions.

## How
Set `hasPackageJson = true` after `installTemplate(...)` completes in `create-app.ts`, and added an automated regression test in `test/production/create-next-app/index.test.ts`.

issue.title: Turbopack removes an IIFE in production builds when its inner callee is annotated /* @__PURE__ */
issue.body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/oenstrom/next-turbopack-pure-iife

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction and install: `npm install`
2. Run `npm run dev` and open http://localhost:3000. The page shows:
   - `annotated IIFE: ran`
   - `plain IIFE: ran`
3. Run `npm run build && npm run start` (Turbopack) and open http://localhost:3000. The page shows:
   - `annotated IIFE: REMOVED`
   - `plain IIFE: ran`
4. For comparison, run `npx next build --webpack && npm run start`. Both lines show `ran`.

The relevant code in `app/page.tsx` is the shape esbuild emits for an IIFE with `keepNames`:

```js
;(/* @__PURE__ */ __name((function annotated() {
  annotatedCalls++
}), 'annotated'))()
```

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** The `/* @__PURE__ */` annotation applies only to the inner `__name(...)` call. The outer call, which invokes the returned function, is not annotated and has side effects, so it must be kept. `next dev` and `next build --webpack` both keep it.

**Current:** `next build` with Turbopack removes the whole IIFE. In the minified chunk, the effect becomes `l(["annotated IIFE: REMOVED", ...])`: the call is gone and the condition is constant-folded.

With `experimental.turbopackMinify: false`, the cause is visible. The parentheses around the annotated inner call are dropped during transformation, so the annotation ends up in front of the outer call:

```js
// input (@radix-ui/react-scroll-area@1.2.18, dist/index.mjs)
(/* @__PURE__ */ __name((function loop() { /* ... */ }), "loop"))();

// Turbopack output, minification disabled
/* @__PURE__ */ __name9(function loop() { /* ... */ }, "loop")();
```

After that, the minifier treats the outer call as pure and removes it.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.6.0: Fri Jul 31 19:16:36 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.161.14~5/RELEASE_ARM64_T6030
  Available memory (MB): 36864
  Available CPU cores: 11
Binaries:
  Node: 22.14.0
  npm: 10.9.2
  Yarn: N/A
  pnpm: 9.1.2
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.5.0-canary.4 // Latest available version is detected (16.5.0-canary.4).
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.3.0
  react-dom: 19.3.0
  typescript: 5.9.3
Next.js Config:
  output: N/A
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

Turbopack, SWC

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next build (local), next start (local), Vercel (Deployed)

### Additional context

Real-world impact: Radix UI publishes its dist with this pattern (built with esbuild `keepNames`), for example:

- `@radix-ui/react-scroll-area` 1.2.18 to 1.3.0: the requestAnimationFrame loop in `addUnlinkedScrollListener` is removed, so the custom scrollbar thumb stops following the scroll position in production. It only updates on the first scroll event of each gesture.
- `@radix-ui/react-menu` 2.1.24/2.1.25 and `@radix-ui/react-select` 2.3.7/2.3.8: the `updateSearch` IIFE in typeahead is removed, so multi-character typeahead does not work.

Versions tested:

- Turbopack `next build` removes the IIFE in 16.3.5, 16.4.0 and 16.5.0-canary.4.
- `next build --webpack` keeps it in 16.4.0 and 16.5.0-canary.4.
- Calling the SWC `minify()` binding from `next/dist/build/swc` directly on the same input removes it in 16.3.5 and 16.3.8 but keeps it in 16.4.0 and 16.5.0-canary.4. So the minifier itself seems fixed, but the Turbopack build pipeline still drops the parentheses before minification.

We see this on Vercel and in local production builds. It does not happen in `next dev`. Our current workaround is to patch the Radix packages to remove the annotation from the invoked IIFEs.

issue.title: turbo-tasks: Add AutoSet and OrderedAutoSet benchmarks
issue.body:
Stacked on #100948.

### What?

Adds a criterion benchmark `auto_set` and an example `memory_usage` to the `auto-hash-map` crate. They compare `AutoSet` with `hashbrown::HashSet` and `OrderedAutoSet` with `indexmap::IndexSet`. The benchmark covers item counts 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 1024, 16 × 1024, 128 × 1024 and 1024 × 1024.

The benchmarked operations are:
- `insert`: build by inserting n items
- `contains_hit`, `contains_miss`
- `iterate`
- `remove_reverse`, `remove_forward`, `remove_random`: remove all items in reverse insertion order, in insertion order, and in a pseudo-random order
- `swap_remove_forward`: remove all items in insertion order with `swap_remove` (ordered sets only)
- `retain`: keep half of the items
- `clone`
- `from_iter`
- `eq`: compare with an identical, separately built set

`cargo run --release -p auto-hash-map --example memory_usage` prints, as CSV, the memory used by each set after inserting n items and after a following `shrink_to_fit()`. It uses the benchmark's item counts plus 3, 5, 6, 7 and 12.

### Why?

The auto sets store up to 32 items in a linear list and switch to a real hash or index set beyond that. These benchmarks show how that trade-off behaves depending on item count, especially around the list/map threshold and for very large sets.

### How?

- All four sets use the same `FxHasher` build hasher and the same `u64` keys, so the comparison measures the storage strategy only. Keys are spread out with a multiply by an odd constant. That map is a bijection, so absent keys are guaranteed for the miss lookups.
- The remove groups and `retain` clone their input in criterion's untimed batch setup. Inputs of 128k items and more are cloned per iteration to bound memory.
- The ordered sets preserve the order on removal: `OrderedAutoSet::remove`, and `IndexSet::shift_remove` to match. That shifts all following items, so `remove_forward` and `remove_random` are O(n²) for them. They only run up to 16k items there, while `AutoSet` and `HashSet` run all sizes. `remove_reverse` is O(n) for all sets.
- `remove_random` uses a fixed-seed Fisher-Yates shuffle, so all sets remove the items in the same order.
- `swap_remove_forward` uses `OrderedAutoSet::swap_remove` and `IndexSet::swap_remove`. It only runs for the ordered sets, because for `AutoSet` and `HashSet` `swap_remove` is `remove`, so it would be identical to `remove_forward`.
- `retain` keeps the keys selected by a key-based predicate, so all sets keep exactly the same items regardless of iteration order.
- `eq` compares two sets built from the same keys in the same order. `OrderedAutoSet`'s equality is order sensitive and compares the two sequences. `IndexSet`'s `PartialEq` ignores the order and looks up each item.
- Large sizes use fewer samples so the full suite stays runnable. Throughput is reported per element.
- Correctness of each setup is asserted outside the timed regions: item counts, hit/miss counts, checksums, removal hits and sizes after remove/retain, and equality.
- `memory_usage` measures `size_of` the set plus its live heap bytes with a counting global allocator. The sets are built by inserting the items one by one and measured right after that, then again after `shrink_to_fit()` on the same set.

### Results

These numbers come from `cargo bench -p auto-hash-map --bench auto_set` in a Linux x86_64 environment, including #100948's `fold` forwarding and out-of-line list → map conversion. The run was interrupted after 524 of 724 cases; the remaining 200 cases (`retain` at 128k and 1M, `clone`, `from_iter`, `eq`) were resumed in that environment. Physical-host continuity across the interruption was not verified. Results depend on machine, runtime conditions and compiled code layout, and the 1M-item cases have only 10 samples. They are meant for orientation, not as regression thresholds. They were measured before this stack was rebased onto `canary` with #101344, which switched `TinyVec` growth and shrinking to `realloc` and came with a newer nightly toolchain, so list-mode timings in particular may differ slightly now. They also predate #100948's later review changes (linear list `retain`/`extract_if`, size-hint-based reservation on list → map conversion, `ShrinkToFit` converting below `MAX_USEFUL_LINEAR_SCAN`), which can affect `retain`, `extract_if`, `extend` and `from_iter` timings. The memory numbers were re-measured after both and are unchanged. Each cell is the auto set's median time as a ratio of the plain set's; < 1 means the auto set is faster.

Takeaways:
- **Up to 32 items:** inserting, removing and retaining are much cheaper than with a real set (often 0.1–0.6×), and iterating an `AutoSet` takes 0.15–0.8× of a `HashSet`'s time. The auto sets also use a fraction of the memory.
- **Lookups near the threshold:** linear lookups get expensive towards 32 items, up to ~2.3–2.5× for hits and ~5.6–5.8× for misses.
- **Order-preserving removal:** `remove_forward` and `remove_random` on the ordered sets are O(n²) once in map mode. At 16k items, `OrderedAutoSet` takes ~0.36 s for `remove_forward` and ~0.2 s for `remove_random`, the same as `IndexSet::shift_remove`. `swap_remove_forward` stays O(n) and is on par with `IndexSet::swap_remove`.
- **`eq`:** `OrderedAutoSet` is 0.09–0.31× `IndexSet` from 8 items on, because it compares the two sequences instead of looking up each item.
- **Cloning** a small `AutoSet` is slower than cloning a `HashSet` (1.5–2.4× up to 32 items), whose clone is a plain memory copy for `Copy` keys.
- **Above 32 items:** the auto sets are mostly on par with their plain counterparts. `AutoSet` iteration takes 0.91–1.01× of `HashSet`'s time and insertion 0.54–1.07×. This iteration benchmark uses `fold`; plain `for` loops still use `next()` and don't get the same optimization. Right after the switch (48 items), the auto sets use more memory than the plain sets, because the map starts with a larger capacity; `shrink_to_fit()` brings `AutoSet` to 640 B vs. 624 B for `HashSet` and `OrderedAutoSet` to 1,432 B vs. 1,416 B for `IndexSet`. After `shrink_to_fit()`, up to 32 items, the auto sets use exactly 16 B plus 8 B per item.

issue.title: Turbopack: add build cache portability e2e test and fix location-dependent tasks
issue.body:
### What?

Adds an e2e test that checks whether the Turbopack filesystem build cache survives moving the project to another directory. It also fixes the first portability problems the test found.

Stacked on #101025, which adds the `executions` counter to turbo-tasks task statistics that this test relies on.

### Why?

A restored build cache should still be valid when the project sits at a different absolute path. That happens with CI checkouts, Docker build contexts, and caches restored into another workspace. Today, moving a project makes many tasks re-execute even though nothing changed. This PR adds a way to measure that and removes some of the causes.

### How?

**Test** (`test/e2e/app-dir/turbopack-portable-build-cache`, Turbopack production builds only, not deploy):

- Each case runs a cold `next build`, a warm build in the same directory, then moves the whole project root (including `.next`) and runs another warm build.
- Every build writes turbo-tasks task statistics (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TASK_STATISTICS`) to a temporary file outside the project. The test collects the functions with `executions > 0`.
  - `cache_miss` isn't enough: it only counts newly created tasks, while a restored task that re-executes after an invalidation counts as a cache hit. #101025 adds the `executions` counter.
- Inline snapshots record the sorted executed function names for the same-dir and moved builds. All `NextConfig` methods are collapsed into a single `NextConfig::*` entry: they depend on the same config cell, and which ones are called depends on the build mode. The snapshots document the current state, and the moved diff should shrink as portability improves. A cold-build execution count check makes sure an empty snapshot means "cached", not "nothing counted".
- Two fixtures:
  - a minimal app;
  - a monorepo whose workspace root is the project root. It covers app and pages routes, a route handler, SSG, a server action, client components from a workspace package, proxy, a `turbopack.rules` loader, `resolveAlias`, jsconfig `paths` outside the app, and relative symlinks.

  The test asserts the route table, the server-actions manifest, and rendered markers on both builds, so a silently dropped feature can't make a snapshot look clean.
- The build env pins `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Inside Docker, `getStorageDirectory()` doesn't persist the generated key in `.next/cache`, so each build would produce a new one. The key is a Turbopack project input, so this would invalidate server-action-dependent work and make snapshots environment-dependent and nondeterministic.
- To keep the snapshots environment-independent, the test also:
  - always installs with pnpm's hoisted linker. The default layout depends on the Node.js version (realpath workaround), which changes which symlinks are resolved;
  - disables telemetry, which reads extra config values.

**Turbopack fixes**, so tasks don't depend on the absolute project location:

- **Source map rewriting** (`turbopack-core` `source_map/utils.rs`):
  - It used to await the entire `DiskFileSystem`, whose cell includes the absolute root, just to build the `turbopack:///[name]/` prefix.
  - It now reads only the filesystem name, through its own task. It reads it only when a source actually uses that prefix, and needs the root only for absolute-path conversion.
  - This removed all relocation-only codegen re-execution (`module_factory_with_code_generation_issue` / `EcmascriptChunkItemContent::new`) in the minimal app.
- **`WriteLinkContent::hash`** reads only the filesystem name instead of the whole filesystem, and no longer requires a `DiskFileSystem`. Hash values are unchanged.
- **`resolve_options`** checks for the configured tsconfig with `get_type()` instead of `metadata()`. A failed `metadata` call's error includes the absolute path, and errors are part of the task output, so the check used to change after a move:
  - files and symlinks count as present;
  - directories, missing entries, and read errors fall back to tsconfig discovery.
- The `trace_task_dirty` feature compiles again (`task_id` was undefined in `make_task_dirty_without_scheduling`).

**Remaining after a move** (visible in the moved snapshots):

- `NextConfig::*` re-runs (`from_string` and its getters), because the serialized config contains absolute paths (`turbopack.root`, `outputFileTracingRoot`, …).
- `DiskFileSystem::new_internal` and writes to the new output location re-run.
- The webpack-loader evaluation pool re-runs; it needs absolute paths to launch Node.js.

### Verification

- Both portability cases pass twice in a row with `CI=1`, and once more with `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS=true`, on top of #101025. The task-statistics snapshots list the same functions as the earlier trace-based ones.
- Existing `server-source-maps`, `tsconfig-path`, `typescript-custom-tsconfig` and `tsconfig-module-preserve` e2e tests pass.
- Rust tests and Turbopack snapshot tests for the touched crates pass.
- Clippy, `pnpm typescript`, prettier and eslint are clean.
- Only measured on Linux x64.
